rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Biomolecules are the chemical basis of life. Carbohydrates supply and store energy and form structural fibres; proteins (from 20 amino acids) act as enzymes, transporters, contractile and defence molecules in four structural levels; lipids store energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) store and express genetic information; enzymes, water and minerals complete the set.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
General carbohydrate ratio: C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1, i.e. (CH2O)n
Endergonic polymerisation (condensation): monomer + monomer → dimer + H2O
Peptide unit: -C(=O)-NH-

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Cellulose is a structural polymer in plant cell walls, not an energy reserve; glycogen (animal) and starch (plant) are the storage forms.  ·  Starch is unbranched amylose + branched amylopectin; both yield maltose on hydrolysis.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: In NEB written answers, pair every macromolecule with BOTH its monomer and its key function to earn full marks.  ·  Protein denaturation is a favourite "application" question (cooking an egg, or fever denaturing enzymes).

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Starch in rice/potato is a storage polysaccharide; glycogen in liver/muscle is the animal reserve.  ·  Cellulose (beta-glucose) forms the cell wall of green plants.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Ribose and deoxyribose differ only by one oxygen atom on C-2; hence RNA vs DNA sugars.  ·  Denaturation unfolds protein (loss of secondary/tertiary structure); it is often reversible at low temperature.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Draw a phospholipid bilayer  ·  Table of 4 macromolecules: monomer, bond, function

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Remember C-H-O-N: C=energy, P=work, L=lipid, N=genetic.  ·  A-T two H-bonds (think "A" has 2 strokes), G-C three.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: How is a triglyceride different from a phospholipid in structure and function?  ·  List the four structural levels of a protein with one example of a quaternary protein.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: High frequency: monomer/polymer matching tables, enzyme action and factors affecting enzymes.  ·  Diagram-based marks: label a phospholipid bilayer and a DNA nucleotide.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Macromolecule monomers  ·  Peptide bond  ·  Denaturation  ·  DNA vs RNA

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Functions: C=energy+structure, P=enzymes/transport/structure, L=storage+membrane, N=heredity+protein synthesis.  ·  A hydrolysis breaks a bond + water; a condensation joins molecules - water.  ·  Enzymes are specific, reversible regulators, not consumed in the reaction.  ·  DNA is the gene; RNA is the messenger/scaffold in protein synthesis.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: A typical human body has roughly the same number of carbon atoms as grains of sand on Earth; carbon is the backbone of all life.  ·  Hemoglobin carries about 1.4 g of oxygen per 100 mL of fully saturated blood.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action and its significance.  ·  Why are essential amino acids called "essential"?  ·  Differentiate amylose and amylopectin and state the test for starch.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Application: explain a disease caused by a biomolecule deficiency.  ·  Do not confuse structural (cellulose) with storage (starch/glycogen) polysaccharides.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: DNA replication and mRNA synthesis link nucleic acids to protein production.  ·  Iodine deficiency enlarges the thyroid; iron deficiency causes anaemia.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Which biomolecule is NOT a true polymer? → C  ·  How many hydrogen bonds are present between G and C in DNA? → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.  ·  Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.  ·  Proteins: polymers of 20 L-amino acids joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Enzyme kinetics  ·  Essential vs non-essential amino acids  ·  Lipid types

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: DNA base pairing: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds)  ·  Essential amino acids (8 in adults, 9 in children) must come from food.  ·  Deficiency of minerals leads to named diseases (Fe→anaemia, I→goitre, Ca→rickets).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Lipids are not polymers; they do not have repeating monomers like the other three macromolecule classes.  ·  A peptide bond forms between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of the next, releasing one water (condensation).  ·  Stress that enzymes lower activation energy; they do NOT supply energy.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Memorise monomer → polymer: glucose→starch, amino acid→protein, fatty acid+glycerol→triglyceride, nucleotide→nucleic acid.  ·  Learn base-pairing and hydrogen-bond counts (A=T=2, G=C=3).  ·  Do 2–3 diagram questions: phospholipid bilayer, peptide bond, a DNA nucleotide ladder.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Link enzyme inhibitors (competitive vs non-competitive) to drug design.  ·  All cells share the same basic biochemical machinery of DNA→RNA→protein (central dogma).  ·  The 20 naturally occurring L-amino acids differ only in their R-group (side chain).
